Prediction target period: from 2025-04-13 to 2025-06-29. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In his keynote address on March 24, 2025, at the NAIC's Spring National Meeting in Indianapolis, newly appointed NAIC President and North Dakota Insurance Commissioner Jon Godfread presented his 2025 strategic roadmap, "Securing Tomorrow: Advancing State-Based Regulation". The meeting, which ran from March 23 to 26, brought together nearly 3,000 participants to discuss the future of the insurance sector. Godfread described the initiative as a "call to action" for collaboration and innovation to ensure sustainable growth, preparedness, and adaptability, thereby securing the U.S. insurance market's global leadership. Key priorities outlined include enhancing catastrophe resilience, modernizing the Risk-Based Capital (RBC) framework, developing frameworks for cybersecurity incidents, advancing consumer privacy protections, enforcing annuity protections, and ensuring access to health insurance. <2> A GlobalData poll conducted across Q4 2024 and Q1 2025 identified the primary reasons for consumers adopting telematics-based insurance policies. According to the findings published on February 27, 2025, the ability to manage the policy digitally, either online or via an app, was the leading motivator for 36.4% of respondents. This was closely followed by the prospect of cheaper premiums, which was cited by 36.2% of participants as their main reason for choosing a telematics policy. <3> In the fourth quarter of 2024, the U.S. commercial insurance market saw continued price increases, though reports on the aggregate rate varied. WTW's Commercial Lines Insurance Pricing Survey (CLIPS) reported an aggregate price increase of 5.6%, a moderation from the 6.1% increase in Q3. [1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8] Conversely, The Council of Insurance Agents & Brokers (CIAB) reported a slight acceleration, with average premium increases rising to 5.4% in Q4 from 5.1% in Q3. [2, 5, 9] A significant development was in the commercial auto liability sector, which experienced its highest price increase ever recorded in the history of CLIPS. [1, 4, 6, 7, 8] This line, along with excess/umbrella liability, saw double-digit increases. [1, 7] CIAB's data corroborated this trend, showing a reversal of moderation in commercial auto premiums, which increased by 8.9% in Q4, up from 8.5% in Q3. [2, 5, 10] This marked the 54th consecutive quarter of premium hikes for commercial auto. [9, 10] Factors contributing to the sustained pressure on commercial auto included increased claims frequency and severity and a decrease in underwriting capacity. [9, 10] While most other lines showed moderation, with some like cyber seeing rate decreases, commercial auto remained a notable exception. [1, 5, 9] <4> A TransUnion report covering the fourth quarter of 2024 revealed a 20% year-over-year increase in auto insurance shopping, a trend primarily driven by consumers seeking lower premium rates. The analysis, published on February 18, 2025, also pointed to an increasing reliance by insurers on traffic court records for a more complete assessment of driver risk. According to TransUnion, an estimated 11% of drivers possess a ratable violation found in traffic court data that is not present on their state motor vehicle records (MVRs). <5> In the first quarter of 2025, a significant legal trend emerged with the filing of several class-action lawsuits against insurers, challenging the methods used to collect and utilize the driving history data of their customers. One notable lawsuit filed in January 2025, and another in February, specifically targeted Allstate and its subsidiary Arity, alleging they secretly collected and sold "trillions of miles" of consumer driving behavior data without informed consent. This data, allegedly gathered from mobile apps and in-car devices, included sensitive information such as geolocation, speed, and braking habits, which was then used to create individual driver profiles. These cases, described as a "trio of new data cases," signify a new legal frontier for the insurance industry regarding data privacy and its application in their processes. <6> On January 7, 2025, a report predicted that auto insurance premiums would continue to rise throughout the year, marking the seventh consecutive year of increases. While the predicted average national increase of 7.5% is less severe than the 16.5% jump seen in 2024, the cumulative effect is expected to push the average annual cost for full coverage to a record high of $2,101. The primary factors driving this trend include the high cost of vehicle repairs and replacement parts, influenced by inflation and supply chain issues. Other contributing elements are an increase in claim frequency and severity, more litigation related to accidents, severe weather events, and a rise in the number of uninsured drivers. Some analyses suggest that while rate increases are slowing, they may still present a financial strain for many households. Projections vary by state, with drivers in New Jersey, Washington, and California expected to see hikes of over 15%. <7> In 2025, the adoption of telematics and Usage-Based Insurance (UBI) is anticipated to shift from being a niche product to a mainstream option for a significant number of drivers. [2] These technologies utilize data from GPS and onboard diagnostics to monitor driving behaviors like speed, braking, and mileage, allowing insurers to offer premiums based on actual driving habits rather than traditional metrics alone. [2, 9] This personalization can lead to significant savings for safer drivers. [5] The market is experiencing rapid expansion, with 2025 growth forecasts showing a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) ranging from 15% to over 31%. [3, 10, 14] However, there are significant discrepancies in market size estimations for 2025, with figures ranging from $15 billion to $83.11 billion, indicating uncertainty in valuation. [10, 14] While becoming more established, a 2024 survey found that telematics policies constituted 14.4% of the personal motor insurance market, suggesting that 'mainstream' in 2025 refers more to widespread availability and insurer focus rather than majority consumer adoption. [12] Key trends fueling this shift include the increased use of AI for risk analysis and a move towards mobile-app-based tracking over hardware devices. [1] Despite the growth, challenges remain; consumer concerns about data privacy and the fair assessment of their driving data are significant hurdles to wider acceptance. [8, 10] <8> The commercial auto insurance market is anticipated to continue its challenging trajectory throughout 2025, characterized by rising premium rates and increasing claim costs. [1, 5] This trend, which has persisted for the last decade, means most policyholders should expect ongoing premium hikes. [1, 5] The market's difficulties are driven by several key factors. Vehicle repair costs remain high due to a combination of labor shortages, supply chain disruptions, and the advanced technology integrated into modern vehicles. [3, 6] Furthermore, the issue of 'social inflation'—marked by increased litigation, more lenient legal environments, broader definitions of liability, and negative sentiment towards large corporations—is exacerbating loss severity. [2, 4, 6] Unsafe driving habits, particularly distracted driving, and widespread driver shortages also contribute significantly to the rising frequency and severity of claims. [2, 7]
